dmm-2021-tiebreaker-01.title: Recursion on F
dmm-2021-tiebreaker-01.body:
Call the starting face $1$ and the opposite face $6$; the other four faces are adjacent to both. Let $G(n)$ be the probability of being at a *specific* one of the four middle faces after $n$ turns.

* The probability of being at face $6$ equals $F(n)$ (face $6$ can be entered only from the four middle faces, exactly like face $1$).
* All probabilities sum to $1$: $2F(n)+4G(n)=1$, so $G(n)=\frac{1-2F(n)}{4}$.
* To be at face $1$ after $n+1$ turns, we must be at one of the middle faces after $n$ turns (total probability $4G(n)$) and then choose face $1$, which has probability $\frac14$. So $F(n+1)=G(n)$.

Therefore $F(n+1)=\dfrac{1-2F(n)}{4}$. From $F(8)=\frac{43}{256}$: $F(9)=\frac{1-\frac{86}{256}}4=\frac{85}{512}$ and $F(10)=\frac{1-\frac{170}{512}}{4}=\frac{171}{1024}$ (already in lowest terms), so $a+b=171+1024=1195$.

**Answer: 1195**
